items.titleTr: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
items.summaryTr: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
items.articleText: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years - Published Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved. Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices. The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056). That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform. Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes. And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing. "Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes. Read more - Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage - Published23 September - Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests - Published5 October The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election. Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike." Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid. Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC. Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment. He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills. "It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas." He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible." With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible". However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing. "This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said. Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election. Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector. Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

items.titleTr: Deutsche Bank launches crypto custody for companies and institutions
items.summaryTr: Clients can store and transfer Bitcoin, Ether and select stablecoins through the bank, which manages their wallets and private keys.
items.articleText: Deutsche Bank launches crypto custody for companies and institutions Clients can store and transfer Bitcoin, Ether and select stablecoins through the bank, which manages their wallets and private keys. Germany’s largest lender, Deutsche Bank, launched its crypto custody service for institutional and corporate clients on Wednesday, according to an announcement shared with Cointelegraph. The bank also signed a memorandum of understanding with Deutsche Asset Management, its majority-owned asset manager, to explore collaboration on tokenized money market funds, crypto asset exchange-traded commodities and stablecoins. Deutsche Bank announced plans to offer the service to institutional and corporate clients in Europe on Sept. 16, pending regulatory clearance. Deutsche Bank’s listing for crypto custody and transfer services in the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) register is dated Oct. 12 and names Germany’s BaFin as its regulator. The service initially supports Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and select stablecoins, including Circle’s USDC (USDC) and EURC (EURC), as well as AllUnity EURAU. Gerald Podobnik, co-head of Deutsche Bank’s corporate bank, told Reuters in October that the bank planned to launch in Germany before expanding to Asian financial centers in 2027. Deutsche Bank partnered with crypto infrastructure provider Taurus in 2023 to develop custody services after applying for a digital asset custody license in Germany. Related: Deutsche Bank-backed AllUnity launches Swiss franc stablecoin CHFAU

items.summaryTr: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
items.articleText: Here’s what happened in crypto today Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation. Today in crypto, Barclays’ BlackRock Bitcoin ETF holdings rose 48% in the third quarter, pro-crypto lawmaker Tom Emmer was elected House Republican minority whip as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and hotter-than-expected US inflation raised concerns about a potential half-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Barclays boosts BlackRock Bitcoin ETF stake 48% as banks expand holdings Barclays reported holding 3.94 million shares in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) at the end of the third quarter, up 48% from the previous quarter. The position in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) was worth about $187 million on Sept. 30, up from $88.5 million for 2.66 million shares on June 30, according to Barclays’ Friday Form 13F filing. “Early readings suggest longer-term holders make up a growing share of the spot bitcoin ETF investor base,” Bitwise analyst Camran Khosravi told Cointelegraph, pointing to increased bank exposure, including at Citigroup. Citigroup reported a new position worth about $119 million in the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC). Its reported IBIT holdings also rose 50% to about 521,000 shares, from 347,000 at the end of June. The filings offer an early indication of changing institutional Bitcoin ETF ownership, with more major banks and hedge funds yet to disclose their third-quarter positions. Institutional investment managers have until Monday to file their third-quarter holdings reports. Crypto ally Tom Emmer elected House GOP minority whip Pro-crypto US Representative Tom Emmer has been elected House Republican minority whip, securing the party’s second-highest leadership position as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January. Emmer beat Texas Representative August Pfluger in a 103-76 secret ballot vote, according to Politico. He previously served as House Republican majority whip and will remain the party’s No. 2 leader, this time under incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan. As minority whip, Emmer will be responsible for rallying Republican votes, coordinating the party’s legislative strategy and helping maintain unity on key bills. “Tom has been one of the strongest advocates for digital assets in Congress, and he has led the fight against a government-controlled CBDC and stood up for American innovators,” GOP Senator Cynthia Lummis said on X. Hot US inflation raises odds of half-point Fed hike in December Crypto industry experts warned on Tuesday that higher-than-expected US inflation could lead to a another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, making borrowing more expensive and potentially discouraging investment in cryptocurrencies. The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% month over month in October, above economists’ forecast of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics - a slower increase than September’s 0.6% rise. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, above the expected 0.2%. Currently, the Federal Reserve holds its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4.00%, after raising it by a quarter-point in September and leaving it unchanged in October. The report came just a few hours after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in London that another core inflation reading of 0.3% or higher could prompt the Fed to consider a larger interest rate hike in December. “In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” Waller said. “Hiking only 25-basis-points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”

items.summary: Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline.

items.titleTr: Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts
items.summaryTr: Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline.
items.articleText: Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline. The collapse of Paraguay’s digital lender Ueno Bank last week left nearly three million customers — roughly 60% of Paraguay’s adults — unable to access their accounts. Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3 after its solvency ratio fell below half the legally required minimum. An investigation uncovered questionable lending practices and deficiencies in credit documentation and accounting. The collapse also triggered a political crisis, with thousands taking to the streets to protest and President Santiago Peña attempting to resign before being impeached and arrested on charges of breach of trust and using his office for personal gain. Paraguay’s peer-to-peer crypto market immediately reflected the turmoil, with some sellers asking for a USDt premium of up to 13%. “USDt is a lifeline for hundreds millions of people in the world,” Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said. For many, the incident sparked uncertainty over savings, wages and the money needed to cover everyday expenses. With the local guaraní (PYG) currency falling 12.3% in a week, some turned to stablecoins to maintain the value of their funds, or just to keep payments moving along. David Eisenmann, founder and chief executive of Paraguayan crypto exchange X4T, tells Magazine the timing made the liquidity need even more pronounced. “The intervention came in the first days of the month,” he says, “exactly when salaries, rent and supplier invoices are due,” adding that many business owners “couldn’t make payroll.” For some, USDt was “suddenly the most liquid money” they had: “This week they learned that having an account isn’t the same as having access to your money.” But beyond another TradFi masterclass in the virtues of self-custody, Ueno’s collapse highlights the growing role of dollar-pegged stablecoins providing an alternative source of liquidity when traditional banks fail. Crypto as a source of liquidity Eisenmann says X4T processed more than $10 million in local on-ramp volume over the 30 days to early November, but some of that activity predated Ueno’s collapse. “The dollar began recovering against the guaraní in October,” he says, “and the Ueno news sped up a move that was already underway.” Related: Stablecoins can drain from banks and nations at lightning speed He says the activity “runs in both directions,” with some customers selling crypto for guaraníes or dollars to cover payments they could no longer make through Ueno, while “demand for USDt and USDC as a dollar store of value has risen sharply.” Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3. Source: Central Bank of Paraguay As of Nov. 9 the Central Bank said 93.1% of customers with Ueno deposits had been repaid. Despite this confidence has been shaken and X4T continued to see higher online inquiries for dollar-denominated stablecoins. In fact, Eisenmann says the level “has not changed significantly” from the week of the collapse. Rhys Hicks, associate analyst at data and analytics company GlobalData, says the digital bank’s failure has shown “how much can go wrong when governance does not keep pace with growth.” That said, he’s not seeing evidence of a mass migration from Paraguayan banks into stablecoins, since other banks “picked up the slack,” and people “seem to have been angrier” with the government than with the banks. “Some consumers will look for different ways to keep their money safe, but I do not see an overwhelming shift to stablecoins yet,” he says. An old impulse, with new rails Seeking dollars when confidence in domestic banks falters is hardly new. In Argentina’s 2001 financial crisis, the government imposed the “corralito,” restricting cash withdrawals from bank accounts, following a run on deposits. Related: Peter Thiel backs crypto-friendly Silicon Valley Bank rival — Report Amid a deepening crisis over the country’s currency peg and sovereign debt, the government later converted dollar-denominated deposits into pesos, reducing people’s savings by about 30% overnight and further damaging confidence in the country’s fraying banking system. Tether CEO calls USDt a lifeline. Source: Paolo Ardoino But stablecoins aren’t decentralized and they are not insulated from the banking system either. During the March 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, stablecoin issuer Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, around 8% of the total, were held at the lender. USDC briefly depegged and fell to 86 cents on secondary markets after Circle said it could not withdraw the funds. A BIS paper on stablecoins and the international monetary system warns that widespread use of dollar-backed tokens could create challenges for monetary sovereignty in emerging markets. Hicks says stablecoins can provide an alternative during periods of political instability and “low trust in the local system” because they are pegged to a more stable currency, like the US dollar. But regulators need to address “transparency” and “consumer protection,” he says, because stablecoin holders don’t benefit from the same deposit guarantees as bank customers, and there is no central bank to step in and make them whole. Eisenmann says he expects the incident to spark more “diversification,” with people “spreading their money across banks, cash and digital assets” instead of relying on a single institution. “How quickly trust in the banks returns will depend on how quickly and transparently the authorities handle the resolution,” he says. Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3 after its solvency ratio fell below half the legally required minimum. An investigation uncovered questionable lending practices and deficiencies in credit documentation and accounting. The collapse also triggered a political crisis, with thousands taking to the streets to protest and President Santiago Peña attempting to resign before being impeached and arrested on charges of breach of trust and using his office for personal gain. Paraguay’s peer-to-peer crypto market immediately reflected the turmoil, with some sellers asking for a USDt premium of up to 13%. “USDt is a lifeline for hundreds millions of people in the world,” Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said. For many, the incident sparked uncertainty over savings, wages and the money needed to cover everyday expenses. With the local guaraní (PYG) currency falling 12.3% in a week, some turned to stablecoins to maintain the value of their funds, or just to keep payments moving along. David Eisenmann, founder and chief executive of Paraguayan crypto exchange X4T, tells Magazine the timing made the liquidity need even more pronounced. “The intervention came in the first days of the month,” he says, “exactly when salaries, rent and supplier invoices are due,” adding that many business owners “couldn’t make payroll.” For some, USDt was “suddenly the most liquid money” they had: “This week they learned that having an account isn’t the same as having access to your money.” But beyond another TradFi masterclass in the virtues of self-custody, Ueno’s collapse highlights the growing role of dollar-pegged stablecoins providing an alternative source of liquidity when traditional banks fail. Crypto as a source of liquidity Eisenmann says X4T processed more than $10 million in local on-ramp volume over the 30 days to early November, but some of that activity predated Ueno’s collapse. “The dollar began recovering against the guaraní in October,” he says, “and the Ueno news sped up a move that was already underway.” Related: Stablecoins can drain from banks and nations at lightning speed He says the activity “runs in both directions,” with some customers selling crypto for guaraníes or dollars to cover payments they could no longer make through Ueno, while “demand for USDt and USDC as a dollar store of value has risen sharply.” Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3. Source: Central Bank of Paraguay As of Nov. 9 the Central Bank said 93.1% of customers with Ueno deposits had been repaid. Despite this confidence has been shaken and X4T continued to see higher online inquiries for dollar-denominated stablecoins. In fact, Eisenmann says the level “has not changed significantly” from the week of the collapse. Rhys Hicks, associate analyst at data and analytics company GlobalData, says the digital bank’s failure has shown “how much can go wrong when governance does not keep pace with growth.” That said, he’s not seeing evidence of a mass migration from Paraguayan banks into stablecoins, since other banks “picked up the slack,” and people “seem to have been angrier” with the government than with the banks. “Some consumers will look for different ways to keep their money safe, but I do not see an overwhelming shift to stablecoins yet,” he says. An old impulse, with new rails Seeking dollars when confidence in domestic banks falters is hardly new. In Argentina’s 2001 financial crisis, the government imposed the “corralito,” restricting cash withdrawals from bank accounts, following a run on deposits. Related: Peter Thiel backs crypto-friendly Silicon Valley Bank rival — Report Amid a deepening crisis over the country’s currency peg and sovereign debt, the government later converted dollar-denominated deposits into pesos, reducing people’s savings by about 30% overnight and further damaging confidence in the country’s fraying banking system. Tether CEO calls USDt a lifeline. Source: Paolo Ardoino But stablecoins aren’t decentralized and they are not insulated from the banking system either. During the March 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, stablecoin issuer Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, around 8% of the total, were held at the lender. USDC briefly depegged and fell to 86 cents on secondary markets after Circle said it could not withdraw the funds. A BIS paper on stablecoins and the international monetary system warns that widespread use of dollar-backed tokens could create challenges for monetary sovereignty in emerging markets. Hicks says stablecoins can provide an alternative during periods of political instability and “low trust in the local system” because they are pegged to a more stable currency, like the US dollar. But regulators need to address “transparency” and “consumer protection,” he says, because stablecoin holders don’t benefit from the same deposit guarantees as bank customers, and there is no central bank to step in and make them whole. Eisenmann says he expects the incident to spark more “diversification,” with people “spreading their money across banks, cash and digital assets” instead of relying on a single institution. “How quickly trust in the banks returns will depend on how quickly and transparently the authorities handle the resolution,” he says. items.articleText: Bitcoin Covenants Part 5: MATT and OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY — How Bitcoin could carry state across transactions OP_CCV embeds contract state directly into Taproot output keys and enforces valid state transitions onchain. This makes it possible to achieve stateful contracts and compact fraud proofs. This is Part 5 in the technical article series about Bitcoin covenants by Cointelegraph Research. To read the previous article click here. MATT (Merkleize All The Things) is a smart contract framework for Bitcoin that enables stateful contracts and scalable fraud proofs. A stateful contract carries information forward across multiple transactions and can update this information as the contract evolves. Standard Bitcoin scripts do not provide this capability, because each transaction is evaluated independently with no memory of previous executions. Every covenant proposal allows state-carrying UTXOs to an extent, as illustrated by scripting languages such as Sapio, which builds on OP_CTV. This works by using addresses to represent a finite state automaton, where transactions function as the state transitions. However, there is no way to elegantly implement numerical logic in this paradigm, a gap filled by MATT, and in particular its proposed implementation through OP_CCV. Because MATT allows committed data to be computed at spend time and re-embedded into the next output, each spend can derive a new state dynamically, instead of choosing from a predetermined set of states. How OP_CCV commits state into a Taproot key To understand the MATT proposal, it is useful to first review how Taproot commits data through public keys. Every Taproot output contains a base public key, called the internal key, which can be cryptographically modified or “tweaked” to commit to extra information. Formally, the tweaked public key is Q = P + t·G, where P is the internal key, G is the generator of the secp256k1 elliptic curve, and t is a tagged hash of P and the committed data. In a regular Taproot output, this commitment typically encodes the Merkle root of a taptree, which contains hidden spending paths. MATT builds on this mechanism to also embed contract state into the key. Instead of embedding complex logic directly in Bitcoin’s scripting language, MATT encodes computation as a sequence of state commitments, and the chain verifies only that each state transition is valid. MATT can be realized through different opcode combinations. The most direct and well-specified implementation relies on OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY (OP_CCV). OP_CCV provides the primitive that makes state-carrying UTXOs feasible within Taproot. OP_CCV allows a script to verify that a Taproot input or output key has been tweaked to commit to a specific piece of state data. The internal key is first tweaked with a hash of the contract’s current state, and then Taproot’s standard taptree tweak is applied on top. The resulting output key therefore commits to both the tapscript (the set of spending conditions) and the current state of the contract. OP_CCV can then enforce what state is carried forward into the next output. It allows the script to inspect the state data provided on the witness stack, perform computations on it, and require that the resulting updated state is correctly re-committed in a specified output. This is how state transitions are enforced on-chain. The stack format is: OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY The opcode supports three modes for checking an output as well as a separate input mode. In default mode, the entire BTC value of the input UTXO is allocated to the specified output; in deduct mode, only a portion equal to the output’s amount is assigned, leaving the remainder available for further outputs; and in ignore mode, the script and data commitment are verified without constraining the amount. Because default and deduct modes are designed to preserve value across checked outputs, transaction fees must be paid through separate fee-paying inputs. A dedicated fee input and change output can be added to the transaction without conflicting with the covenant’s constraints. This prevents the accidental burning of funds that can occur in more primitive covenant implementations, such as OP_CTV or SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT. It also addresses a major limitation of presigned-transaction-style covenants, which typically define amounts upfront and therefore cannot accommodate dynamic fee adjustments or partial unvaults. OP_CCV + OP_CAT: Merkle Proofs and Fraud Proofs When OP_CCV is combined with OP_CAT, the full MATT framework becomes even more expressive. OP_CAT enables byte concatenation in Script, which makes it possible to construct and verify Merkle proofs directly on-chain. Two distinct Merkle trees are associated with a Taproot output in such an arrangement. The first is the familiar Taproot script tree (the taptree), whose leaves are the contract’s spending scripts. The second is a separate state tree, whose leaves are the contract’s data, such as the intermediate steps of a computation. The OP_CCV + OP_CAT script can verify a Merkle proof against the current state tree root, compute the updated root after a transition, and use OP_CCV to force the next output to commit to it. This construction enables fraud-proof systems with a slashing condition in which a long computation is committed off-chain, and only the specific disputed step (with its path in the binary tree) needs to be revealed and verified on-chain. Similar systems exist as optimistic rollups on other blockchain systems: the full computation runs off-chain, and the on-chain contract only intervenes when someone raises a challenge. Fraud proofs require that the computation be compiled down to a binary circuit or equivalent step-by-step representation that can be committed to in a Merkle tree. OP_CCV + OP_CAT would avoid the need for the Lamport one-time signatures and pre-signed transaction graphs that BitVM relies on to enforce state consistency. Beyond fraud proofs, the OP_CCV and OP_CAT combination also has implications for vaults. OP_CCV alone can implement vaults, but when combined with OP_CAT, it allows fully featured vaults that are essentially equivalent to the functionality proposed by OP_VAULT. As James O’Beirne, the author of OP_VAULT, has noted, OP_CCV represents a more general and robust design that effectively supersedes his earlier proposal. In the next article in this series, we will move on from general covenant proposals to review application-specific opcodes such as OP_VAULT, OP_UNVAULT, and OP_EVICT. Each of the opcodes are designed to solve a specific problem rather than provide broad programmability. Magazine: Bitcoin holders have received eCash — What can you do with it?

items.titleTr: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
items.summaryTr: Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah is being tried on the charge of "publishing false news" and potentially faces imprisonment.
items.articleText: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom' - Published A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation. Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge. The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists". Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left". She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next." Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder. Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down. After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge. At the opening session, Attalah's defence team requested the judge's recusal, arguing that he had "already formed a conviction in mind against the defendant", Mada Masr cited its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar as saying, external. The judge went into recess before adjourning proceedings for a week to allow the court to consider the defence's request, he added. Mada Masr also said Attalah's appeal against last month's conviction was scheduled to take place on 25 November. Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders' 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention. While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country. It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza. In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government. "It's much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation," she said. "People need to know, people need to consume information and you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're killing the newsrooms that do it properly." In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh - constituting its entire newsroom - were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week. They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood. Egypt's former president Mohammed Morsi – who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood – was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown. On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped. He also said the case against Attalah "raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial". "We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information," Al-Kheetan said. "The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern." Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability. It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington's annual $1.3bn military aid package. The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday. "We didn't discuss it today," Rubio said. "But… like anything else in foreign policy, there's always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States." "That doesn't mean you agree with everything another government does," he went on, adding that he was not "opining about their journalists". items.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
items.summary: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.

items.titleTr: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
items.summaryTr: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
items.articleText: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter - Published Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia. Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola. The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack. All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday. - Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada - Published6 days ago "Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added. The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare". He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather". Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC. "When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said. Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area. The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found. "Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement. "We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola. The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack. All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday. - Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada - Published6 days ago "Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added. The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare". He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather". Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC. "When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said. Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area. The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found. "Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement. "We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

items.articleText: CoreWeave stock jumps 15% premarket after Q3 revenue beats estimates CoreWeave’s third-quarter revenue rose 168% to $3.66 billion, beating analyst estimates by 3.4%. Its revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion. CoreWeave shares jumped 15.27% in premarket trading Wednesday after the AI cloud provider reported third-quarter revenue that beat analyst estimates. The shares traded at $56.12 as of 12:50 pm UTC, trimming the stock’s year-to-date decline to 32%, according to Yahoo Finance. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in third-quarter revenue after the market closed on Tuesday, up 168% from $1.36 billion a year earlier. Revenue came in about 3.4% above the $3.54 billion consensus estimate compiled by Google Finance. The company also reported a revenue backlog of about $132.5 billion as of Sept. 30. The figure includes revenue CoreWeave expects to recognize under existing customer contracts, subject to delivery and service availability. In April, CoreWeave announced a multiyear agreement with AI developer Anthropic to provide computing capacity for its Claude models. Days later, CoreWeave signed a $6 billion deal with quantitative trading company Jane Street to supply cloud infrastructure for trading and research. CoreWeave started as a crypto miner and began shifting to AI infrastructure in 2019. Related: CoreWeave shows how crypto-era infrastructure quietly became AI’s backbone

items.titleTr: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
items.summaryTr: The country begins a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new cases are recorded.
items.articleText: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status - Published Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free. It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi. He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died. Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation. "Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak. "This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X. - What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? - Published15 September Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October. All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission. Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers. Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday. Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown. Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries. Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams. The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country. In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens. Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings. The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries. Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June. But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE. The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures. Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August. The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way. - Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in its history - Published17 August Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. items.title: FSB urgest Turkey to tighten crypto oversight, set stablecoin rules
items.summary: The Financial Stability Board cited progress on crypto licensing and urged stronger enforcement and cooperation with foreign regulators.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: FSB urgest Turkey to tighten crypto oversight, set stablecoin rules
items.summaryTr: The Financial Stability Board cited progress on crypto licensing and urged stronger enforcement and cooperation with foreign regulators.
items.articleText: FSB urgest Turkey to tighten crypto oversight, set stablecoin rules The Financial Stability Board cited progress on crypto licensing and urged stronger enforcement and cooperation with foreign regulators. The Financial Stability Board (FSB) urged Turkey to tighten its oversight of crypto markets and adopt dedicated rules for stablecoins. In a peer review published on Wednesday, the global financial watchdog said Turkish authorities had made progress by introducing registration and licensing requirements for crypto service providers. The report was part of the FSB’s regular program of country reviews and assessed Turkey’s progress in implementing the board’s 2023 global recommendations on crypto and stablecoins. It followed a broader 2025 review that found gaps in how jurisdictions had implemented those recommendations. The FSB recommended that Turkey begin monitoring crypto-related risks to financial stability under a formal framework, strengthen supervision and enforcement, and improve cooperation and information sharing with foreign regulators. Turkey’s Capital Markets Board introduced licensing and operational requirements for crypto exchanges and custodians in March 2025, including minimum capital thresholds. The FSB said Turkey had introduced safeguards including requirements to segregate assets held in custody and a ban on domestic crypto payments. The safeguards help limit the spread of crypto-related risks to banks and payment systems. Authorities also launched a centralized platform to monitor crypto activities. The FSB’s 2025 review found that Turkey had finalized rules for crypto assets but lacked a dedicated stablecoin framework. In June 2025, Turkey’s Finance Ministry outlined plans to introduce additional transaction checks and limits on stablecoin transfers to combat money laundering. Related: Turkey tightens crypto rules with source, purpose checks on transfers

items.summary: Zcash fell nearly 15% amid a broader sell-off in privacy coins, a day after Grayscale pledged $1 million to ecosystem initiatives.

items.titleTr: Zcash falls below $1,000 for first time since September
items.summaryTr: Zcash fell nearly 15% amid a broader sell-off in privacy coins, a day after Grayscale pledged $1 million to ecosystem initiatives.
items.articleText: Zcash falls below $1,000 for first time since September Zcash fell nearly 15% amid a broader sell-off in privacy coins, a day after Grayscale pledged $1 million to ecosystem initiatives. Zcash (ZEC) fell to a two-month low of $962.85 on Wednesday, a day after Grayscale pledged $1 million to nonprofits and projects supporting the Zcash network. As of 12:20 pm UTC Wednesday, Zcash’s 13.5% drop led 24-hour losses among the 100 largest cryptocurrencies by market capitalization and was down 24.5% over seven days. The decline was part of a broader crypto sell-off that left Bitcoin (BTC) down 5.8% and Ether (ETH) down 11.6% over the same period, according to CoinGecko. Crypto prices fell further Tuesday after US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from the previous month, above economists’ 0.3% forecast. Zcash lets users send shielded payments that keep sender and recipient addresses and transaction amounts out of public view. Zcash helped drive this year’s rally in privacy coins, gaining 138% in the 30 days to Sept. 7. It remains the largest privacy coin by market value, accounting for about 60% of the $28 billion category tracked by CoinGecko. The category’s combined market value fell about 7% over 24 hours. ZEC traded above $1,370 as recently as Friday, when Zcash activated its NU7 upgrade. The upgrade cut the target time between blocks from 75 seconds to 25 to speed up transaction confirmations. It also made about 12,224 ZEC held in the network’s original privacy pool unspendable. Grayscale converted its Zcash Trust into a US spot exchange-traded fund (ETF) that began trading on NYSE Arca on Aug. 25. The fund recorded about $15 million in net outflows in November through Monday, following about $46 million in October, according to SoSoValue. Related: Zcash devs propose another block time cut days after NU7 upgrade

items.title: CFTC Sanctions Eight Individuals for Acting as Unregistered Associated Persons of Foreign Introducing Brokers
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC Sanctions Eight Individuals for Acting as Unregistered Associated Persons of Foreign Introducing Brokers
items.articleText: Release Number 9324-26 CFTC Sanctions Eight Individuals for Acting as Unregistered Associated Persons of Foreign Introducing Brokers November 09, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced eight orders filing and settling charges against Michael Talento, Anthony Tyler Williams, Quillan Roberto Black, Christopher Williams, Michael Levi Peters, Jordan Taylor Morgan, Lewis Matthew Neal, and Tyler Evan MacKechnie for acting as unregistered associated persons of unregistered foreign introducing brokers. According to the orders, the introducing brokers engaged in the solicitation of orders for off-exchange leveraged or margined retail foreign currency and retail commodities transactions with U.S. customers who were not eligible contract participants. The respondents solicited those customers without registering as associated persons of the introducing brokers, as required. Under the orders, the respondents must cease and desist from engaging in their illegal conduct. They also are barred for two years from registering with the Commission in any capacity or acting as a principal, agent, or employee of any CFTC registrant. Each order also recognizes the penalty the respondent owes in a related Securities and Exchange Commission proceeding. These orders relate to a prior Commission order sanctioning Netrios LP Ltd. and Red Acre Ltd. for facilitating illegal off-exchange commodity transactions with U.S. customers. [See CFTC Press Release No. 9263-26] The SEC has filed and settled charges against the respondents based on the same underlying conduct. The CFTC thanks the SEC for its assistance. -CFTC-

items.title: CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation
items.articleText: Release Number 9323-26 CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation November 05, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today issued an interpretation (“Interpretation”) of the requirement that designated contract markets (“DCMs”) provide competitive, open, fair, and impartial access to their members and persons with trading privileges under Commission Regulation 38.151(b) (“Impartial Access Requirements”). “Derivatives markets must operate on a uniform basis at a national scale in order to achieve the purposes set out in the Commodity Exchange Act,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “Geographic access restrictions are inconsistent with those purposes and the Act’s impartial access requirements.” DCMs must cease domestic geographic restrictions that violate the Impartial Access Requirements within 30 days, or else submit to the Division of Market Oversight (“Division”) an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. Further, within 30 days, DCMs should ensure that intermediaries accessing their markets are not impeding and are complying with the DCM’s Impartial Access Requirements, or else submit to the Division an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. The Commission will consider the facts and circumstances of any particular case in connection with potential Commission action. -CFTC-

According to the letter, a derivatives clearing organization may use a trust company for daily settlements if it treats the trust company as it would a settlement bank under applicable CFTC requirements. -CFTC-

items.title: CFTC and USDA Sign MOU to Protect Integrity of American Agricultural Markets
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC and USDA Sign MOU to Protect Integrity of American Agricultural Markets
items.articleText: Release Number 9321-26 CFTC and USDA Sign MOU to Protect Integrity of American Agricultural Markets November 04, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture today announced their signing of a Memorandum of Understanding intended to safeguard the integrity of U.S. agricultural markets. The MOU will allow the CFTC and USDA to harmonize policies and practices to better share information and increase access to risk management tools. The agreement will also assist both agencies with monitoring and identifying structural or potential systematic risks, among other things. “For decades, America’s agricultural community has relied on our markets to hedge risk, manage uncertainty, and plan for the future,” said CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig. “I’m proud that the CFTC and USDA have formalized this partnership through an MOU that will strengthen protections for America’s farmers, ranchers, and producers while expanding opportunities to manage risk through more efficient data sharing. I commend Secretary Rollins for her partnership and commitment to a more coordinated regulatory approach that safeguards the integrity of our markets and ensures they continue serving the agricultural community that feeds and clothes our nation.” “Faster and more transparent data sharing between USDA and CFTC is critical to helping our farmers and ranchers navigate an ever-changing market,” said USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins. “This MOU builds upon USDA’s ongoing data modernization efforts and allows our agencies to collaboratively identify risks and improve responses to market events. Breaking down barriers between government agencies to deliver for our customers is a hallmark of this administration and I am looking forward to the successes this MOU will bring.” -CFTC-

items.title: CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud
items.articleText: Release Number 9320-26 CFTC Secures Court Order Directing Texas Man and His Company to Pay Over $13 Million in Commodities Fraud November 03, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered a default judgment against defendants Walter Dunning Larrick III and Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC for their participation in a commodities fraud scheme. In entering the default judgment, the court found the defendants fraudulently solicited and misappropriated more than $3 million from participants. The court found the defendants falsely represented they would use participant funds to trade futures and options, including those involving natural gas, oil, and gold; made material misrepresentations and omissions about the profitability of commodity trading with them; and issued false account statements to conceal their misconduct. The court further found the defendants misappropriated participant funds by making payments to existing participants in a manner akin to a Ponzi scheme, paying Larrick’s personal expenses, and sending funds to offshore accounts in Costa Rica. The court ordered the defendants to pay a $9,767,625 civil monetary penalty and $3,255,875 in restitution. It also permanently enjoined them from further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and Commission regulations, as charged, and imposed permanent trading and registration bans. The default judgment resolves all claims in the CFTC’s 2023 complaint. [See CFTC Press Release No. 8768-23.] -CFTC-

items.title: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
items.articleText: Release Number 9319-26 CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures November 03, 2026 WASHINGTON — CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig today released a statement announcing that perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities can begin trading for the first time on designated contract markets that are dually registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as notice-registered national securities exchanges to trade security futures products. Key excerpts from Chairman Selig’s statement: “Today, perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities (the ‘Equity Perps’) can begin trading for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges. … “This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery. I believe that bringing these types of innovative products into our regulated markets ensures that American investors and traders can access these products within the protections of the CFTC’s proven regulatory framework, rather than being forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues. … “The Equity Perps build on the foundation of the [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000] and the [CFTC-SEC Memorandum of Understanding]. For too long, regulatory uncertainty left innovative products, such as security futures and equity perpetual futures, stranded in what SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins has aptly described as a regulatory ‘no man’s land’ due to a lack of harmonization between the agencies. The CFTC and SEC have turned the page on that era, and are committed to delivering regulatory clarity for innovative products and a clear path to market, rather than more casualties of jurisdictional disputes.” Read Chairman Selig’s full statement here. -CFTC-

items.title: CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading
items.articleText: Release Number 9318-26 CFTC to Host Roundtable on 24/7 Trading October 28, 2026 WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced it will host an industry roundtable Dec. 15 to discuss issues related to the viability of derivatives markets moving to 24/7 trading. The dialogue will build upon the CFTC’s Request for Comment earlier this summer on 24/7 trading. The CFTC’s roundtable will provide a public venue for dialogue on the evolving market structures shaping derivatives markets, including overnight trading, tokenization, infrastructure and staffing needs, and operational readiness. Participants will convene from across the industry to discuss how the Commission can promote responsible innovation while protecting market participants and preserving the integrity and resilience of U.S. derivatives markets. “I have been consistently clear: under my leadership, the CFTC will not take a one‑size‑fits‑all approach to 24/7 trading. Market structure evolves best through thoughtful and responsible progress, and that’s exactly why we’re hosting a roundtable to hear directly from industry on their views for 24/7 trading across different asset classes,” Chairman Selig said. The roundtable will take place at CFTC’s headquarters in Washington. Information regarding the agenda, speakers, and registration will be posted at a later date. This event will be open to the public and livestreamed on CFTC.gov. Please note the number of in-person participants may be limited, and visitors will be subject to security checks. Members of the public are welcome to submit speaker nominations to [email protected]. -CFTC-

items.title: ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026
items.verification: Birincil kaynak
items.titleTr: ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026
items.articleText: Release Number 9317-26 ICYMI: Agricultural Leaders and Market Participants Join CFTC Chairman Selig in Overland Park, Kansas for AgCon 2026 October 27, 2026 WASHINGTON — Last week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Risk Management Center at Kansas State University co-hosted the 2026 Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference (AgCon) in Overland Park, Kansas. The two-day conference brought together industry leaders, policymakers, and market participants to examine critical issues facing the agricultural economy, developments in derivatives markets, and the risk management tools American farmers, ranchers, and agribusinesses depend on. Conference Highlights CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig joined K-State President Richard Linton to welcome participants on opening day. CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig addressed conference attendees, “I have spent a lot of time this year traveling around the country and talking to farmers and ranchers working hard each day to provide the food, feed, and fiber we depend on throughout our country and the world. I’ve met with farmers, ranchers, agribusinesses, and energy producers in Iowa, Texas, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Florida, and now, I’m with all of you here in Kansas.” [Watch Chairman Selig’s full remarks here.] Following Chairman Selig’s remarks, panelists examined the relationship between cash and derivatives markets, evolving commodity contracts, and the importance of effective hedging tools for agricultural producers. There were also panels where industry representatives addressed access to agricultural credit and the financial challenges facing producers and merchants. Additional afternoon discussions focused on rising production costs, fluctuating commodity prices, supply chain disruptions, and broader pressures on the farm economy. In addition, conference participants engaged in discussions about emerging market developments, including perpetual futures, 24/7 trading, and tokenized collateral, and their implications for agricultural risk management. CFTC Chief Advisor Alex Titus and White House Council of Economic Advisers Member Aaron Hedlund also examined the U.S. economic outlook, agricultural trade, and policies shaping American agriculture. The first day concluded with a keynote address from U.S. Department of Agriculture Deputy Secretary Stephen Vaden. U.S. Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas opened the second day with a morning keynote address on agricultural policy and legislative priorities facing American producers. The morning continued with discussions on agricultural prediction markets, the use of data in modern commodity markets, and developments in event contracts. In addition, panelists examined superintelligence, information advantages, and market integrity, including the implications of emerging technologies for market participants and regulators. Chairman Selig joined Futures Industry Association President and CEO Walt Lukken for a fireside chat examining the Commission’s priorities, the evolving regulatory landscape, and developments shaping derivatives markets. The conference concluded with discussions on enhancing public understanding of markets through data and customer education, followed by a panel examining clearing, market access, and the role of intermediaries in derivatives markets. Chairman Selig delivered closing remarks, concluding AgCon2026. -CFTC-
